title: AI heavies PM with an open threat
full_text:
OpenAI has issued an ultimatum in a bid to strong-arm Anthony Albanese into breaking his promise to protect creative industries, declaring it will not even consider investing in domestic AI training or renewable energy if the government refuses to water down copyright laws.
Amid grassroots backlash to the spread of data centres and warnings that AI is developing fast enough to endanger humanity, Assistant Technology Minister Andrew Charlton told The Australian that the AI and data centre revolution would rival the mining boom’s economic output from 2003 to 2013, but provide more long-lasting benefits through productivity gains.
There was $8.7bn of investment in data centres in the March quarter, accounting for 17 per cent of all private sector spending. Treasury predicts AI will add $116bn to GDP over the next decade, an estimate Dr Charlton regards as “cautious”.
“Australia has secured decades of economic advancement by embracing new sources of growth ... The mining boom flowed mainly through two states and a few sectors. AI flows through every business in the country,” Dr Charlton said.
But despite pledges from the Prime Minister that the government will force AI data centres to be “net generators, not net users” of energy, the maker of ChatGPT has rejected any prospect of discussions over renewables unless Labor backs down from its commitment to creatives.
In an exclusive interview with The Australian in Canberra, OpenAI’s senior vice president, Ann O’Leary, suggested that if the Albanese government did retreat on copyright, Australia would be the first country outside the US to host artificial intelligence model training for the AI giant. “No other place in the world has done (AI training) this yet, and so the question is: is Australia going to be the first? And that’s really a copyright question more than a renewable energy question,” Ms O’Leary said.
“Our company isn’t ready to have that conversation if we can’t get through the gating problem of the copyright barriers.” Ms O’Leary said countries such as Australia and Canada were good targets – after negotiations with the UK stalled over copyright – because they were US allies.
“When we look at the geopolitical dynamic and we think of countries who really want to see a diversification of where training may occur, there’s a lot of interest in making sure that happens in an allied country,” she said.
She said OpenAI was “kind of blocked” from pushing into the UK with training data centres because its government refused to water down its copyright laws, and the company’s approach to negotiations had not changed.
“I don’t think that we have necessarily changed and part of what I think we’re grappling with is we are still training primarily in the United States because of the legal framework, but we do think that there’s an opportunity,” she said.
“We’ve been welcomed by your Prime Minister and others who are open to this conversation. So we’re walking through the door that’s been opened.” The Prime Minister and Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen have been wrestling with the states over planned national standards that would have data centres rely on renewable power, in a bid to avoid community backlash in the US and elsewhere.
Ms O’Leary, formerly chief of staff to Democratic presidential hopeful Gavin Newsom and adviser to Hillary Clinton, said her company ; would not be able to build any AI training centres without a loosening of copyright, powered by renewables or otherwise.
“We will not be able to build a … training centre here if the copyright law is as it exists,” she said. “And so the lack of detail (on renewables) isn’t because we wouldn’t be serious about it, but the options that we’ve seen from the government so far, frankly, wouldn’t allow us to train here.” AI training is the computing required to build the models instead of merely running and serving them up to users.
Training compute is the cutting edge of computing capacity that has AI labs racing to secure the latest and greatest Nvidia chips to get an edge over their competitors. The Biden White House sought to restrict the export of these chips to China to give US companies a leg-up.
Speaking before OpenAI made its ultimatum, Dr Charlton warned that achieving long-term dividends from the boom would require a more active role for government than what was needed when China’s rapid growth massively increased the prices of Australia’s natural resources.
“That opportunity is before us again, and we must capture the benefits of the AI investment boom while acting with sophistication to minimise the risks,” Dr Charlton said.
“AI is not just another technology. It is becoming a factor of production in its own right, amplifying the value of labour and capital and reshaping how economies create prosperity.” While the economic output would rival the mining boom, Dr Charlton said the benefits of AI would “stretch further than mining”. He said that, unlike the mining boom, the AI boom would compound. “The mining boom was a one-off level shift that peaked and receded,” he said. “AI productivity gains compound: at a point a year, AI exceeds the mining boom’s entire effect inside a decade and keeps going. With nine in ten businesses yet to adopt, the reorganisation of Australian business has barely begun.” Dr Charlton said Australia needed to develop more AI capability to take advantage of the boom. “The mining boom came with an income engine attached: we owned the ore, the world paid us for it, and the money flowed in,” he said. “The AI boom, so far, runs the other way: the chips are imported, the models are foreign-owned, and the equipment bill helped deliver our first goods deficit since 2017. Mining generated prosperity – but AI only pays the countries that adopt fastest, adopt deepest, and own a piece of the stack. The boom is guaranteed; the dividend is not.” Anthropic general counsel Jeff Bleich said copyright was one of the critical issues that “need to be worked out” before the AI juggernaut could build data centres in Australia.
